The company makes different designs depending on whether the awning is meant to block sunrises or sunsets. The key factor here is the street address: odd-numbered addresses face east, and even-numbered addresses face west. Therefore, clients with even-numbered addresses will receive the sunset awning design.

First, I should access the spreadsheet located at '/Users/icyfeather/Projects/Magentic-One/gaia-val/4d51c4bf-4b0e-4f3d-897b-3f6687a7d9f2.xlsx'. Once I have the spreadsheet open, I need to identify the column that contains the street addresses. This is crucial because without knowing which column has the addresses, I can't proceed to count the even-numbered ones.

Next, I'll write a Python script using the pandas library to read the spreadsheet data. The script should extract the 'Street Address' column and then count how many of these addresses are even-numbered. To do this, I'll loop through each address, split the string to get the house number, and check if it's even. If it is, I'll increment the count.

After writing the script, I'll execute it to get the count. The result should tell me how many clients will receive the sunset awning design. Once I have the number, I'll present it along with a brief explanation of the logic used to arrive at that conclusion.

I think I've covered all the necessary steps. Now, I'll proceed to write the script and execute it to find out the number of clients with even-numbered addresses.

The agent assumed the first part of the address was the house number but didn't account for possible street types or suffixes, resulting in an inaccurate count.
